title: Pound-Drever-Hall Feedforward for Trapped-Ion Optical Qubits
authors: Jia-Yang Gao, Jianwei Lee, Morteza Ahmadi, Manas Mukherjee
abstract: Laser phase noise is one of the limiting factors that dictate gate fidelities and coherence times in trapped-ion quantum systems. Previous studies have reported that when the Rabi frequency of an ion qubit is close to the servo-bump phase-noise frequency, the driving laser limits the fidelity and coherence time. This issue has typically been mitigated by choosing a Rabi frequency outside the servo-bump region. However, this constrains the usable range of gate speeds and can limit the achievable fidelity. To address this issue, we developed an active phase-noise stabilization system for a barium-ion optical-qubit laser at 1762 nm, employing a fiber electro-optic modulator (EOM) with an electrical feedforward servo. Our results demonstrate that this setup, based on the Pound-Drever-Hall (PDH) feedforward method, can suppress servo-bump phase noise by 15 dB near the bump peak frequency in our locking system. The laser phase noise is analyzed using delayed self-heterodyne interferometry (DSHI). We further tested the stabilized laser on an optical qubit and observed a clear improvement in coherence time based on the measured amplitude decay of Rabi oscillations, even when the Rabi frequency lies within the servo-bump bandwidth. This technique can be readily adapted to other optical qubits with minimal modifications.
summary: The paper addresses laser phase noise, a major hurdle for trapped-ion qubits, by implementing an active Pound-Drever-Hall feedforward stabilization system. This technique successfully suppresses detrimental servo-bump phase noise near the operating frequency. The results confirm that this stabilization significantly improves qubit coherence time and gate fidelity across previously restricted operational regimes.
main_problem: Laser phase noise is a critical limiting factor for achieving high gate fidelities and coherence times in trapped-ion quantum systems.
main_result: The implementation of Pound-Drever-Hall (PDH) feedforward stabilization successfully suppresses servo-bump phase noise by 15 dB, allowing optical qubit operations to maintain coherence even when the Rabi frequency is near this problematic noise region.
method: The authors employed an active phase-noise stabilization system using a fiber electro-optic modulator (EOM) and electrical feedforward servo, validated through Delayed Self-Heterodyne Interferometry (DSHI).
model_or_system: The experiment uses a trapped-ion optical qubit platform based on Barium ions ($	ext{Ba}^+$) at 1762 nm. The analysis models the qubit dynamics using Pauli-transfer matrices and stochastic differential equations to track coherence decay.
key_observables: Coherence time ($T_2$), gate fidelity ($\epsilon_{	ext{avg}}$), Rabi oscillation amplitude decay, and measured phase noise suppression (15 dB).
important_parameters: Rabi frequency relative to the servo-bump bandwidth; stabilization level of 15 dB; operating wavelength of 1762 nm.
main_assumptions: The technique's applicability was experimentally verified for optical qubits, and coherence time analysis relies on fitting $\log_{10} T_2$ vs. $\Delta 	ext{dB}$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup involving PDH stabilization and DSHI measurement, comparing noise suppression results with linewidth measurements.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying laser phase noise as a limitation to detailing the PDH feedforward technique, measuring its performance via DSHI, and finally demonstrating the resulting improvement in qubit coherence time through Rabi oscillation analysis.
why_interesting: This work provides an essential experimental blueprint for mitigating technical noise sources (laser phase noise) that fundamentally limit the achievable gate fidelity in trapped-ion quantum computing architectures.

A delayed fiber is used to match the optical phase between the two arms, and the output serves as the seed laser for the thulium-doped fiber amplifier (TDFA). For intensity stabilization, the signal from a photodetector is used for electrical feedback to control the RF drive of the acousto-optic modulator (AOM). FIG. 2: DSHI measurements of the phase noise and linewidth of the 1762 nm laser. Figure 2a shows that when the BNC cable length is not optimal (300 m), the phase noise cannot be fully reduced. Figure 2b demonstrates that at the optimal cable length (325 m), the feedforward servo suppresses the servo-bump phase noise by up to 15 dB. Figure 2c shows that the feedforward servo does not broaden the laser linewidth, ensuring minimal impact on the qubit transition.

FIG. 3: Rabi Oscillation measurements. Figure 3a compare the Rabi oscillations with and without phase noise stabilization and perform T2 fitting. From the data, we observe that T2 is longer when the beam is stabilized. The D-state probability at the first π-time improves, demonstrating a corresponding enhancement in gate fidelity. Figure 3b compare the frequency scan excitation spectra with and without phase noise stabilization (pi time used: 22.1us). The additional off-resonant excitation is clearly observable (circled by a dashed green line), with its shape determined by the servo noise and locking bandwidth.

FIG. 4: Log-linear scaling of T2 coherence time with servo-bump phase-noise reduction. The plot shows the measured coherence time T2 as a function of the servo-bump phase-noise reduction (in dB). A log-linear fit shows an improvement factor of approximately 1.21× in T2 per dB of noise suppression. Blue points (Rabi frequency ≈132 kHz) are used for the fit, while red points (≈345 kHz) are shown for comparison.

FIG. 5: Phase-noise spectrum and simulated phase-noise-limited average π-gate infidelity versus frequency. Blue curves: calibrated phase-noise PSD (left axis, dBc/Hz). Orange open circles: 1 −F (ϕ) avg for resonant π pulses (logarithmic right axis), where at each marker the Rabi frequency equals that frequency and tπ = 1/(2fR). The full measured spectrum, not just the PSD value at f = fR, enters each finite-time calculation. Left and right panels show PDH feedforward disabled and enabled. The Rabi frequency is scanned from 20 to 450 kHz with one common calibration factor.
